title: Job Chapter 6 Quiz - Multi-Level
description: An enhanced quiz on Job chapter 6 with Easy, Medium, Hard, and Theological levels. Each level has 15 carefully crafted questions. Choose your difficulty and dive in!

easy.title: Job Chapter 6 Quiz - Easy Level
easy.description: Perfect for beginners! Test your basic knowledge of Job Chapter 6.

questions.question: In Job 6, which of the following appears FIRST in the chapter?
options: Job wishes his grief were weighed
Job speaks of arrows of the Almighty
Job asks if the wild ass brays when it has grass
Job longs for God to destroy him
questions.correctAnswer: Job wishes his grief were weighed
questions.explanation: Job first speaks about wishing his grief were weighed in Job 6:2, which appears before the other events mentioned.

questions.question: Who answered and spoke in Job 6:1?
questions.explanation: Job answered and said as stated in Job 6:1.

questions.question: According to Job 6:3, what would be heavier than the sand of the sea?
questions.explanation: Job says his calamity would be heavier than the sand of the sea in Job 6:3.

questions.question: What is said to be 'within me' in Job 6:4?
questions.explanation: Job states that the arrows of the Almighty are within him in Job 6:4.

questions.question: What does Job compare the poison to in Job 6:4?
options: That which drinketh up his spirit
questions.correctAnswer: That which drinketh up his spirit
questions.explanation: The poison is described as that which drinketh up Job's spirit in Job 6:4.

questions.question: According to Job 6:5, does the wild ass bray when it has grass?
questions.explanation: Job asks rhetorically if the wild ass brays when it has grass, implying it does not, in Job 6:5.

questions.question: What question does Job ask about eating unsavoury food in Job 6:6?
options: Can that which is unsavoury be eaten without salt?
Is unsavoury food good for the soul?
Does unsavoury food nourish the body?
questions.correctAnswer: Can that which is unsavoury be eaten without salt?
questions.explanation: Job questions if unsavoury food can be eaten without salt in Job 6:6.

questions.question: In Job 6:7, what does Job say the things his soul refused to touch are like?
questions.explanation: Job says the things his soul refused to touch are as his sorrowful meat in Job 6:7.

questions.question: What does Job long for God to grant him as stated in Job 6:8?
options: The thing that he longs for
questions.correctAnswer: The thing that he longs for
questions.explanation: Job expresses a wish that God would grant the thing he longs for in Job 6:8.

questions.question: What does Job say he would do if God destroys him in Job 6:9?
options: He would let loose his hand and cut him off
He would harden himself in sorrow
He would not conceal the words of the Holy One
questions.correctAnswer: He would let loose his hand and cut him off
questions.explanation: Job wishes God would let loose his hand and cut him off as stated in Job 6:9.

questions.question: What does Job say about the words of the Holy One in Job 6:10?
questions.explanation: Job states he has not concealed the words of the Holy One in Job 6:10.

questions.question: True or False: Job compares his calamity to being heavier than the sand of the sea.
questions.explanation: Job says his calamity would be heavier than the sand of the sea in Job 6:3.

questions.question: True or False: Job asks if an ox lows over his fodder in Job 6.
questions.explanation: Job asks if the ox lows over his fodder in Job 6:5.

questions.question: True or False: The text says Job desires to live a long and prosperous life.
questions.explanation: Job expresses a wish for God to destroy him, not for a long prosperous life, as seen in Job 6:8-9.

questions.question: True or False: The text says Job’s spirit is strengthened by the terrors of God.
questions.explanation: Job says the poison drinks up his spirit and terrors of God set themselves against him, which indicates distress, not strengthening (Job 6:4).

medium.title: Job Chapter 6 Quiz - Medium Level
medium.description: Ready for more? Apply biblical truths from Job Chapter 6 to real-life situations.

questions.question: What is Job questioning about his strength?
questions.explanation: Job 6:11 states, 'What is my strength, that I should hope?' indicating his deep questioning of his ability to maintain hope.

questions.question: What does Job 6:14 suggest should be shown to an afflicted person?
questions.explanation: Job 6:14 mentions, 'To him that is afflicted pity should be shewed from his friend,' highlighting the importance of compassion.

questions.question: In Job 6:12, what does Job compare his strength to?
questions.explanation: Job 6:12 asks, 'or is my flesh of brass?' suggesting he feels his strength is not substantial.

questions.question: According to Job 6:15, how have Job's brethren treated him?
questions.explanation: Job 6:15 states, 'My brethren have dealt deceitfully as a brook,' indicating betrayal.

questions.question: What does Job 6:18 say about the paths of the brooks?
questions.explanation: Job 6:18 explains, 'the paths of their way are turned aside; they go to nothing,' emphasizing futility.

questions.question: What does Job express a desire for in Job 6:8?
questions.explanation: Job 6:8 states, 'Oh that I might have my request; and that God would grant me the thing that I long for!' indicating his longing.

questions.question: In Job 6:17, what happens to the brooks when they warm up?
questions.explanation: Job 6:17 mentions, 'What time they wax warm, they vanish,' illustrating their temporary nature.

questions.question: What does Job 6:19 say about the troops of Tema?
questions.explanation: Job 6:19 states, 'The troops of Tema looked,' indicating hope and anticipation.

questions.question: What is implied about Job's friends in Job 6:14?
questions.explanation: Job 6:14 suggests that his friends have forsaken the fear of God, implying a lack of kindness.

questions.question: What is Job's metaphor in Job 6:6 regarding unsavory food?
questions.explanation: Job 6:6 questions whether something unsavory can be eaten, illustrating his deep despair.

questions.question: In Job 6:9, what does Job wish God would do?
questions.explanation: Job 6:9 expresses Job's despair as he wishes God would let loose His hand and cut him off.

questions.question: What do the companies of Sheba do in Job 6:20?
questions.explanation: Job 6:20 states, 'They were confounded because they had hoped,' indicating disappointment.

questions.question: According to Job 6:4, what does Job feel is affecting his spirit?
questions.explanation: Job 6:4 states, 'the poison whereof drinketh up my spirit,' indicating a deep spiritual affliction.

questions.question: Job believes that he has concealed the words of the Holy One according to Job 6:10?
questions.explanation: Job 6:10 mentions, 'for I have not concealed the words of the Holy One,' indicating he has been open.

questions.question: Job compares his sorrowful meat to something in Job 6:7. Is it something he desires?
questions.explanation: Job 6:7 states, 'The things that my soul refused to touch are as my sorrowful meat,' indicating rejection rather than desire.

hard.title: Job Chapter 6 Quiz - Hard Level
hard.description: Challenge yourself with deep analysis and cross-biblical connections from Job Chapter 6.

questions.question: According to Job 6:21, what causes Job's friends to be afraid?
questions.explanation: Job 6:21 states, 'For now ye are nothing; ye see my casting down, and are afraid,' indicating the cause of their fear is seeing his downfall.

questions.question: In Job 6:22, what does Job deny asking from his friends?
options: Bring unto me or give a reward
questions.correctAnswer: Bring unto me or give a reward
questions.explanation: Job 6:22 says, 'Did I say, Bring unto me? or, Give a reward for me of your substance?' showing Job denies asking for these.

questions.question: What does Job ask in Job 6:23 that he has not requested?
options: Deliver me from the enemy's hand or redeem me from the mighty
Heal my wounds or cleanse my sin
Build me a house or give me land
questions.correctAnswer: Deliver me from the enemy's hand or redeem me from the mighty
questions.explanation: Job 6:23 states, 'Or, Deliver me from the enemy's hand? or, Redeem me from the hand of the mighty?' showing Job denies asking for these deliverances.

questions.question: In Job 6:24, what does Job request from his friends?
options: Teach me, and I will hold my tongue
questions.correctAnswer: Teach me, and I will hold my tongue
questions.explanation: Job 6:24 says, 'Teach me, and I will hold my tongue: and cause me to understand wherein I have erred,' indicating Job desires instruction.

questions.question: According to Job 6:25, how does Job describe 'right words'?
questions.explanation: Job 6:25 states, 'How forcible are right words!' which means right words have great power.

questions.question: In Job 6:27, what wrongful actions does Job accuse his friends of?
options: Overwhelm the fatherless and dig a pit for your friend
Steal from the poor and lie to the just
Ignore the needy and curse the righteous
questions.correctAnswer: Overwhelm the fatherless and dig a pit for your friend
questions.explanation: Job 6:27 says, 'Yea, ye overwhelm the fatherless, and ye dig a pit for your friend,' accusing friends of harming vulnerable and trusted ones.

questions.question: What does the Hebrew word 'ra'ah' (רַע) in Job 6:27 mean?
questions.explanation: The Hebrew word 'ra'ah' in Job 6:27 carries the meaning of 'to do evil or harm,' consistent with the context of overwhelming the fatherless and digging a pit.

questions.question: Which literary device is primarily used in Job 6:16-17 where the brook is described as blackish by ice and snow that vanish when warm?
questions.explanation: Job 6:16-17 uses metaphor comparing deceitful friends to a brook blackened by ice and snow that vanish when warm, symbolizing their unreliability.

questions.question: Which Old Testament passage connects to the theme of friends being false or unreliable as in Job 6:15-18?
questions.explanation: Psalm 41:9 speaks of a close friend who betrays, paralleling Job 6:15-18's theme of deceitful friends.

questions.question: Which New Testament verse echoes the theme of suffering and friends' betrayal found in Job 6:14-20?
questions.explanation: 2 Timothy 4:16 mentions being deserted by friends, echoing Job 6:14-20 about abandonment in suffering.

questions.question: What comes immediately before Job's statement in Job 6:21 about his friends being afraid?
options: They were confounded because they had hoped
My brethren have dealt deceitfully as a brook
Teach me, and I will hold my tongue
questions.correctAnswer: They were confounded because they had hoped
questions.explanation: Job 6:20 states, 'They were confounded because they had hoped; they came thither, and were ashamed,' which immediately precedes verse 21.

questions.question: In Job 6:30, what does Job claim his 'taste' cannot discern?
questions.explanation: Job 6:30 says, 'Is there iniquity in my tongue? cannot my taste discern perverse things?' showing Job claims he can discern evil.

questions.question: What is the rhetorical question Job asks about his strength in Job 6:12?
options: Is my strength the strength of stones? or is my flesh of brass?
Is my wisdom greater than the elders?
Do I have the power to command armies?
Can I control the winds and the sea?
questions.correctAnswer: Is my strength the strength of stones? or is my flesh of brass?
questions.explanation: Job 6:12 asks, 'Is my strength the strength of stones? or is my flesh of brass?' questioning his own physical endurance.

questions.question: How does Job describe the sorrowful state of his soul’s nourishment in Job 6:7?
options: The things that my soul refused to touch are as my sorrowful meat
My soul feasts on rich food and wine
I find joy in the smallest blessings
My soul is as a garden in bloom
questions.correctAnswer: The things that my soul refused to touch are as my sorrowful meat
questions.explanation: Job 6:7 says, 'The things that my soul refused to touch are as my sorrowful meat,' indicating deep grief affecting appetite.

questions.question: True or False: In Job 6:29, Job asks his friends to return, assuring them his righteousness is in his words.
questions.explanation: Job 6:29 states, 'Return, I pray you, let it not be iniquity; yea, return again, my righteousness is in it,' confirming Job’s plea for reconciliation and assertion of righteousness.

theological.title: Job Chapter 6 Quiz - Theological Level
theological.description: Deep biblical theology from Job Chapter 6 that unites all believers. Explore foundational truths about God, creation, and humanity.

questions.question: What doctrine does Job 6:4 teach about God's nature?
options: God's sovereignty includes His righteous judgment and affliction
God is uninvolved in human suffering
God is limited by human understanding
God shows favoritism only to the righteous
questions.correctAnswer: God's sovereignty includes His righteous judgment and affliction
questions.explanation: Job 6:4 describes 'the arrows of the Almighty' and 'the terrors of God' setting themselves against Job, illustrating God's sovereign power to bring affliction as part of His righteous judgment.

questions.question: What doctrine about human sin and suffering is taught in Job 6:14?
options: True friendship requires pity for the afflicted, reflecting reverence for God
Suffering is always a punishment for hidden sin
Friends should avoid the suffering to prevent contamination
The fear of God is unrelated to how one treats the afflicted
questions.correctAnswer: True friendship requires pity for the afflicted, reflecting reverence for God
questions.explanation: Job 6:14 states that pity should be shown to the afflicted from friends but laments that his friends abandon the fear of the Almighty, linking reverence for God with compassionate friendship.

questions.question: What doctrine of human frailty and hope is Job 6:11 teaching?
options: Human strength and hope are limited and fragile in the face of suffering
Human strength is equal to divine strength
Hope is independent of human strength
The end of life is irrelevant to faith
questions.correctAnswer: Human strength and hope are limited and fragile in the face of suffering
questions.explanation: Job 6:11 questions what strength Job has to hope or prolong life, emphasizing human frailty and limited hope amid calamity.

questions.question: Which divine attribute does verse Job 6:9 specifically demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Job 6:9 expresses a desire for God to 'let loose his hand, and cut me off,' indicating God's sovereign control over life and death.

questions.question: Which divine attribute is highlighted in Job 6:24?
questions.explanation: Job 6:24 asks to be taught and for understanding of error, reflecting an appeal to God's wisdom as the source of true knowledge.

questions.question: How does Job 6:15-18 connect to broader biblical themes about human reliability?
options: It illustrates the instability and fleeting nature of human help
It affirms that human allies are always dependable
It teaches that human help supersedes divine assistance
It denies the existence of betrayal in human relationships
questions.correctAnswer: It illustrates the instability and fleeting nature of human help
questions.explanation: Verses 15-18 compare Job's brothers to unreliable streams that vanish, emphasizing the biblical theme that human help is often unstable and not ultimately dependable.

questions.question: What redemptive-historical theme does Job 6:25-26 prepare for in Scripture?
options: The power and limitation of human words compared to divine truth
The ultimate victory of human wisdom over suffering
The irrelevance of speech in the life of faith
The necessity of silent endurance without explanation
questions.correctAnswer: The power and limitation of human words compared to divine truth
questions.explanation: Job 6:25-26 highlights the force of right words but also the futility of arguing with one in despair, prefiguring New Testament teaching about the sufficiency of Christ's word over human debate.

questions.question: What combined doctrine do verses Job 6:2 and Job 6:3 teach about the nature of human suffering?
options: Human suffering is weighty beyond measure and can silence speech
Suffering is light and easily dismissed
Suffering is unrelated to divine judgment
Suffering enhances human eloquence and joy
questions.correctAnswer: Human suffering is weighty beyond measure and can silence speech
questions.explanation: Job 6:2-3 speak of grief being heavier than the sand of the sea and words being swallowed up, teaching that suffering is profound and can overwhelm human expression.

questions.question: What combined doctrine about friendship and divine reverence do Job 6:14 and Job 6:27 teach?
options: True friendship requires fear of God and compassionate support; betrayal is sin against both
Friendship is independent of reverence for God
Betrayal is justified by human weakness
Divine reverence excuses neglect of the afflicted
questions.correctAnswer: True friendship requires fear of God and compassionate support; betrayal is sin against both
questions.explanation: Job 6:14 calls for pity from friends reflecting fear of God, while 6:27 condemns overwhelming the fatherless and digging pits for friends, showing betrayal violates both friendship and divine reverence.

questions.question: What doctrine about human strength and divine wisdom do Job 6:12 and Job 6:13 together teach?
options: Human strength and wisdom are limited and insufficient apart from God
Human flesh and stones are equally strong
Divine wisdom is irrelevant to human hope
questions.correctAnswer: Human strength and wisdom are limited and insufficient apart from God
questions.explanation: Job 6:12 questions if his strength is like stones or brass, and 6:13 asks if his help and wisdom are gone, teaching human frailty and the need for divine wisdom.

questions.question: Sceptics claim Job 6:22-23 shows Job demanding material reward. What does the passage actually teach?
options: Job denies asking for material reward or deliverance, emphasizing his innocence
Job demands riches and rescue from enemies
Job admits guilt and asks for punishment
Job is silent about his needs
questions.correctAnswer: Job denies asking for material reward or deliverance, emphasizing his innocence
questions.explanation: In Job 6:22-23, Job explicitly denies saying 'Bring unto me' or asking for reward or deliverance, highlighting his protest against false accusations rather than demanding material help.

questions.question: What doctrine about the human condition and divine justice is taught in Job 6:8-10?
options: Suffering can lead to a desire for death but also a recognition of God's justice
God's justice is irrelevant to suffering
Humans can escape suffering by their own strength
questions.correctAnswer: Suffering can lead to a desire for death but also a recognition of God's justice
questions.explanation: Job 6:8-10 shows Job longing for death yet still respecting God's holiness and justice, illustrating the complex human response to suffering within divine justice.

questions.question: Which divine attribute is most clearly demonstrated in Job 6:30?
questions.explanation: Job 6:30 questions if there is iniquity in his tongue and if he cannot discern perverse things, emphasizing the sanctity and moral purity expected before God, reflecting His holiness.

questions.question: What combined theological insight do Job 6:6 and Job 6:7 provide about human suffering and experience?
options: Suffering can make even what was once refused to be consumed, illustrating the bitterness of affliction
Suffering does not affect human appetite or spirit
Human desires are unaffected by affliction
questions.correctAnswer: Suffering can make even what was once refused to be consumed, illustrating the bitterness of affliction
questions.explanation: Job 6:6 asks if unsavory food can be eaten without salt, and 6:7 says things his soul refused to touch became his sorrowful food, symbolizing how suffering perverts human experience.

questions.question: How do Job 6:19-20 contribute to the narrative arc of hope and despair in Job's story?
options: They show that even external groups hoped for Job but experienced shame, emphasizing the depth of his trial
They demonstrate universal support for Job
They highlight Job's triumph over enemies
They depict Job's isolation from all nations
questions.correctAnswer: They show that even external groups hoped for Job but experienced shame, emphasizing the depth of his trial
questions.explanation: Job 6:19-20 mention the troops of Tema and companies of Sheba looking and waiting, but ultimately being confounded and ashamed, underscoring the profound nature of Job's suffering and dashed hopes.
